sections.text: Who looks equally upon honour and dishonour, loves friends and foes alike, abandons all initiative, such is he who transcends the Qualities.
And he who serves Me and only Me, with unfaltering devotion, shall overcome the Qualities, and become One with the Eternal.
For I am the Home of the Spirit, the continual Source of immortality, of eternal Righteousness and of infinite Joy.

Okay, so I will be discussing the last four verses of chapter 14. Chapter 14 is the Gunatraya Vibhaga Yoga. We have discussed and basically found so far that in this Prakriti, this manifest world, everything has these three gunas, which are the signature of Prakriti: Sattva -- the light, the knowledge, the awareness; Rajas -- the activity; and Tamas -- inertia.
These three gunas bind this supreme self, which has no limitations, to this limited being. These qualities belong to my body, mind and intellect. Once the consciousness attaches to this, it takes upon itself all the limitations of Prakriti.
So I, the ego, am right now conditioned by this body, mind, and intellect. Therefore I have all the limitations of body, mind, and intellect. Therefore I go through sorrows and happiness, pleasant and unpleasant experiences, conducive and unconducive situations.
Because each entity by itself has its own priorities and its own situations. The world remains the world -- one person sees it as very positive, the other sees it as very negative. Depending on their own conditioning, one who goes beyond these three gunas will be beyond all these conflicts and sorrows.
So what we have seen is that these three gunas also belong to my mind. It is my mind which is sometimes sattvic, sometimes rajasic, or sometimes tamasic. Depending on the qualities of my mind, Ill see this world as Sattvic, Rajasic, or Tamasic.
My experiences will be driven by the moods of my mind. So if I can get over this, if I can introspect and vigilantly monitor the moods of my mind, I will be able to rise above the situations I am facing. The situation remains the same, but I can change the mood of my mind, and that will change my reaction to the situation.
But the ultimate goal is to go beyond the three gunas all the time. So the verse we have seen: udasina avad asino gunaihi yo na vichalyate -- one who is indifferent to these gunas and does not get swallowed by them. Guna vartanta iti eva avatishtati na ingate. What is happening in this world is nothing but the play of the gunas.
Gunas are the ones acting in this world. Guna guneshu vartante iti matvaa na sajjate -- knowing that what is happening is the gunas of my senses and the gunas of this world of objects reacting with each other. When I have an experience, it is an interaction between the gunas of my senses, my body, my mind, and the gunas of the objects.
So when I come across a conducive situation, I feel happy. In an unconducive situation, Im not happy -- but the one who knows that the self that I am does not get disturbed by it remains steady. This verse 23: Guna vartanta iti eva avatishtati na ingate -- knowing that these are all the play of the gunas only, and nothing to do with me the self, he does not move from his state of bliss.
He is always in the state of bliss as the self. When we hear whats happening in Tahrir Square in Egypt, does it really make me so upset that I couldnt sleep at night? I may have my opinion whether theyre good or bad for the world, but thats all it is -- Im a third-party observer. If I can do the same thing for everything happening to me in my own Tahrir Square, then I will be the same way.
Thats all its saying. So now, Arjuna had asked three questions. One: what are the marks of a person who has gone beyond the gunas? This is exactly similar to chapter two, where he asks, what are the qualities of a person who is Buddhi-sthita, established in wisdom? Same thing here: how do I know that person has gone beyond the gunas? Then, how does he move around and talk in this world? And lastly, how did he do it? The one who is beyond the gunas, knowing that this is the play of gunas only, does not get disturbed.
Thats the mark of him. What will be his behavior? We have seen in the following verses: Sama dukha sukhaha svasthaha sama loshta ashma kanchanaha tulya priya apriya dhiraha tulya ninda atma samstutih. We have seen this in Bhagavad Gita before -- the quality of a person whose Buddhi is established in the supreme self and not in this limited self.
When things occur in this life, such a person sees that its this ego reacting with the world outside, and therefore Sama dukha sukhaha -- whether the condition is conducive or non-conducive, he remains the same. He sees that we dont have big riots when seasons change. From spring we move to fall and then winter.
We dont have riots in the streets about that. Why? Because we accept thats how nature is. After spring, fall has to come, and after fall, winter has to come.
We adjust to it. In our life, we are not accepting this -- we always want a hundred percent happiness all the time, and therefore we get all disturbed. But the person who knows this, just like I know that fall will come after spring and winter will come after fall, knows that after every happy occasion there is something unhappy, non-conducive.
Those of you educated by Indian TV know this all the time, right? So Sama dukha sukhaha svasthaha. He remains Svasthaha -- balanced, not affected by Sukha or Dukha. Knowing this is a temporary interaction between the gunas of myself as body, mind, intellect, and the world.
When the economy is doing well, we are all very happy -- everybody talks about the party, about how much money they made in the stock market. Now we all talk about, I dont know what Obama is doing. Why doesnt he think about me? Thats the nature of this world.
Sama loshta ashma kanchanaha -- he also sees no greater value in one thing of this world than another. Now does that mean that if somebody asks for one rupee, he gives away a thousand-dollar note? No. A transaction in this world is a transaction between me, the limited being, and the world.
That is what is called Vyavahara. And Vyavahara should be appropriate to the situation. However, such a person doesnt see one transaction as inherently more important than another.: when you were a little kid, a game card -- one was more valuable than the other.
I grew up in India, so we used to have Parle bottle tops. There was a value to each one -- a Parle cap had greater value than a certain other brand, right? Anybody remember that? In those days, your wealth was those bottle tops, and if somebody took them away from you, it was devastating. But when you grow out of it, all those bottle tops are worth nothing to you.
One who sees the world that way knows that each thing has its own value in that particular transaction at a particular time. Therefore we say, you may have a styrofoam cup and somebody has a gold cup. Both are thirsty and going to a lake -- which one is more valuable than the other? As long as there is an emptiness which can fetch water -- for me, thats all that counts.
At that moment, the value of gold and the value of styrofoam is exactly the same, depending on which can fetch more water. So sama loshta ashma kanchanaha -- he does not give greater value to one or the other, knowing that the value only belongs to the exchange or the utility in that particular transaction. Tulya priya apriya -- this one, obviously, we all can use.
He remains the same when something comes which is dear to me or not dear to me, because it is not in my control. We struggle through in this economy, go through interviews and proposals, and we come out and everybody says, Rajan, you really did a fantastic presentation. I feel so good -- until I hear that my competition got the project.
Things will come to you by their own nature. They are not depending on my efforts alone; theyre coming to me by their own nature. And I react to that as my right or my misfortune, depending on what is coming to me.
You can really see it: I say, boy, Rajan, you did so good -- but when you dont, I think you should have prepared a little better. Rajan, I think this time you were not really ready; you should have prepared more. Whether its good or bad.
What happened? Suddenly my success now defines whether I was good or not. We were reading about Steve Jobs. He threw away all the rules of business -- no focus groups, no surveys, nothing. What do people know about what they want? I will tell them what they want. So he worked completely contrary to other peoples business models, as taught in Harvard and everywhere else.
And his is the most successful company. So now we say, lets look at the Steve Jobs model, how he built the company. You have to remain the same whether people are praising you or not.
They praise you simply because it is the nature of the world, not yours. And then the next verse says Mana apamana yoho tulyaha tulyo mitraha aripaksha yoho. Continuing the same teaching.
Bhagavan says such a person who has gone beyond the gunas is acting in this manner. He is working in this world as a normal person, but in his mind, he sees all this as a temporary occurrence -- nothing that he controls. His duty is to act according to dharma in each situation.
Mana apamana yoho -- this is obviously very important to us because we get hurt very easily. Mana and apmana -- honor and dishonor -- are at our mental level. This is truly at our minds level.
Sometimes the person who is telling you something had no intention of insulting you or hurting you. But you take it that way because your mental state was such that you received it that way. If Im supremely confident, people say something critical and I think, dont worry about it.
But if Im already shaky, then somebody says, Rajan, youre not doing well. Then I collapse right there. So it is not the world, but my mind that decides whether this is mana or apmana.
He is so established in himself that whatever comes from the world, he just takes it at face value and moves on. Mitraha aripakshayoho -- this is another important quality. These are my friends and these are my enemies.
My relationship may be different with each person, but my inner stance toward them should remain the same. That does not mean that when enemies are attacking your country, you say, well, well receive you the same way we receive our allies. At that time, your Vyavahara -- your appropriate action -- is to protect your country.
But just as Gandhi said, I hate the British government but not the British people. Its not the person you are reacting to, but the action you are reacting to. Therefore, tulya mitra aripaksha -- equal toward friend and foe.
Aripaksha -- the foes, the enemies. Mitra -- friend. We all know this.
Sarva Arambha parityagi -- we have seen it before, and this is the most difficult one. He gives up all endeavors, all efforts. Sarva Arambha parityagi -- this sounds like complete death.
If I stop doing everything, its a complete death. I will stop all my endeavors and efforts when I die. Ed thats exactly what theyre asking you to do.

These concluding verses answer Arjunas final question: How does one transcend the gunas? Verse 25 continues the portrait: mānāpamānayoh tulyah, equal in honor and dishonor, tulyo mitrāri-pakshayoh, the same toward friend and foe. Then comes the challenging phrase: sarvārambha-parityāgī, one who has abandoned all undertakings. This sounds like death itself! But the teaching clarifies: it means giving up the SENSE of personal doership, not the actions themselves. Continue to work, but know that the gunas alone act while you remain the witness. Verse 26 then gives the method: mām cha yo avyabhichārena bhaktiyogena sevate, one who serves Me with unwavering devotion transcends the gunas and becomes fit for union with Brahman.
The chapters final verse (27) reveals Krishnas ultimate identity: brahmanah hi pratishthā aham, I am the abode of Brahman, amritasya avyayasya cha, of immortality and imperishability, shāshvatasya cha dharmasya, of eternal dharma, sukhasyaikāntikasya cha, and of absolute bliss. This is where the journey ends, or rather, where the illusion of journey dissolves. Today, practice sarva-ārambha-parityāga in a practical way: choose one activity and perform it completely, but without the sense that I am doing this. Let the hands move, let the mind think, but rest as the awareness in which all this happens. Notice how this does not diminish the quality of action, often it improves it, as you noted from the Karma Yoga teachings. The one who has nothing to prove, nothing to gain, acts with perfect freedom. Can you taste that freedom today, even in one small task?
